tip: आदाब अर्ज़ है (aadaab arz hai) is literally 'respects are presented' – a courtly Urdu-style greeting you'll hear among Urdu speakers and in formal, old-school settings.
होने वाली है (hone vaali hai) = 'is about to happen'. Verb + वाला (vaala) marks something on the verge – the same वाला (vaala) that usually means 'the one who'.
-कर (-kar) on a verb means 'having done it': ताला लगाकर (taala lagaakar = having locked). Hindi links actions this way where English says 'and then'.
Position words follow their noun: कल तक (kal tak) is literally 'tomorrow by' = 'by tomorrow'. Flip the English order every time.
तो (to) after a word isn't 'then' – it stresses that word: उसे तो (use to = as for him) – he, of all people, already knew.
कम से कम (kam se kam) is literally 'less than less' – Hindi's way of saying 'at least'. The mirror phrase ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा (zyaada se zyaada) = at most.
काश (kaash) = 'if only'. काश मुझे पहले पता होता (kaash mujhe pehle pataa hotaa = if only I'd known earlier) – the bare -ता (-taa) form marks a wish that didn't come true.
ही (hi) narrows to 'only/exactly': मुझसे ही होगा (mujhse hi hoga) = it will get done only by me. It's sharper than English 'just'.
अच्छा (achchhaa) literally means 'good', but opening a sentence it works as 'okay / oh / I see' – here it's just moving the conversation along, not praising anything.
After ने (ne), the verb agrees with the object. मैंने रोटी खाई (mainne roti khaai = I ate bread, f sg). मैंने रोटियाँ खाईं (mainne rotiyaan khaaeen = plural). Subject doesn't matter.
तो (to) adds attitude – contrast or emphasis, like 'well' or 'really': तुमने तो कमाल कर दिया (tumne to kamaal kar diya) = you really pulled it off.
Hindi adds 'went' to say something is fully over: ख़त्म हो गई (khatm ho gayi = became finished, went). That little गई (gayi = went) marks the change as complete.
भी (bhi = also/too) sits right after the word it stresses: तुम भी चलो (tum bhi chalo) = you come too. Move भी and the emphasis moves with it.
करता हूँ (kartaa hoon) is present tense – literally 'I call' – but it means 'I'll call'. Hindi uses the plain present for things you're about to do.
You don't find things in Hindi – they 'meet' you: चाबी कहीं मिल नहीं रही (chaabi kaheen mil nahin rahi = the key isn't turning up anywhere). The same verb मिल (mil) is used for meeting people.
जी (ji) after a name adds respect: सरला जी (Sarla ji) works like a built-in 'ma'am'. It also makes yes and no politer: हाँ जी (haan ji), ना जी (naa ji).
बस (bas) here isn't the vehicle – it means 'enough, no more'. The same word also means 'just/only', so context decides which बस (bas) you're hearing.
No ने (ne) on the doer here: विकास (Vikas) just गया (gayaa = went). Going acts on nothing, so the doer stays plain. Ne appears only when the action lands on a thing.
Doubling often intensifies: सुबह-सुबह (subah-subah = morning-morning) means very early, at the crack of dawn. Repeating a word is a normal grammar move in Hindi.
Past-tense doers take ने (ne): श्याम ने नई नौकरी शुरू की (Shyam ne naee naukree shuru kee = Shyam started a new job). Ne appears only when the action lands on something.
बेच दीं (bech deen = sold off) ends in a nasal sound because किताबें (kitaaben = books) is feminine plural – the verb tracks the books, and the tiny dot is its only plural clue.
Joy happens TO you in Hindi: ख़ुशी हुई (khushee huee = happiness occurred). You aren't glad – gladness arrived. The set phrase for being pleased to meet someone.
No 'was inspected' – Hindi says the check happened: जाँच हुई (jaanch huee = inspection happened). When the doer doesn't matter, things simply occur.
English words become verbs with किया (kiyaa = did): बुक किया (buk kiyaa) = booked. The loanword stays a noun; करना (karnaa = to do) does the verb work – recharge kiyaa, cancel kiyaa.
'Without' wraps its noun from both sides: बिना किसी मदद के (binaa kisee madad ke) – binaa before, ke after. English says 'without' once; Hindi closes the bracket.
Hindi has no verb 'drive' – you make the vehicle go: गाड़ी तेज़ चलाई (gaadee tez chalaaee = drove the car fast). चलाना (chalaanaa = make move) also runs shops and machines.
जी (jee) after a name adds warmth and respect: सुनीता जी (Suneetaa jee). It attaches to any name – and even to yes and no: haan jee, nahin jee.
'Told me to rest' = आराम करने को कहा (aaraam karne ko kahaa) – literally 'said for doing rest'. Orders and requests use karne ko, not a plain to-verb.
खा लिया (khaa liyaa) adds लेना (lenaa = take) to eating – it signals the food is finished, gone. Plain खाया (khaayaa) just says eating happened, with no sense of completion.
'Reached Shimla' sounds like it acts on Shimla, but पहुँच गए (pahunch gaye) takes no ने (ne) – arriving counts as pure motion in Hindi, like going and coming.
